title: Public Health Nurse Roles and Qualifications
body:
## What it is
The public health nurse (PHN) is a nurse working for a local or national health office or a public school, whatever the job title. The role covers many hats at once, and the exam likes to ask which hat a described action belongs to.

## Roles and what each looks like
- Planner/programmer: identifies health needs, priorities and problems of individuals, families and the community.
- Nursing care provider: cares for the sick and disabled at home, clinic, school or workplace.
- Manager/supervisor: writes and carries out the nursing plan and leads people to solve their own health problems.
- Community organizer: motivates participation and starts or joins community development work (see [[Community Organizing (COPAR) Basic Principles]]).
- Service coordinator: works with individuals, families and groups to link them to services.
- Health educator/counselor/trainer: teaches, counsels, trains rural health midwives, speaks as a resource person.
- Health monitor: tracks the status of clients through repeated contacts.
- Role model: lives a healthy lifestyle visibly.
- Change agent: motivates changes in health behavior.
- Reporter/recorder/statistician: records every intervention, updates the database, analyzes data (links to [[Epidemiology and FHSIS]]).
- Researcher: uses observation, interview, survey and physical exam for assessment.

## Qualifications (as listed in the handout)
- BSN graduate and registered nurse, in good physical and mental health.
- Interest and willingness to work in the community; able to work with other disciplines and community members.
- Able to analyze factors that affect population health, apply the nursing process and mobilize community resources.
- Leadership potential, resourcefulness, active membership in professional nursing organizations.
- Salary grade given in the handout: 15.

## How the exam asks about it
Match the action to the role: a nurse teaching midwives is trainer; a nurse who tallies cases is recorder/statistician; a nurse who motivates smoking cessation is change agent.

## Related topics
[[Community Health Nursing Basics]], [[Department of Health (DOH) Concepts and Functions]].

## Check against your textbook
Salary grade and the exact qualification list can change with civil service rules.

title: Health Sector Reform Agenda and FOURmula One
body:
## What it is
The Health Sector Reform Agenda (HSRA) is described as the overriding goal of the DOH. FOURmula One for Health (2005-2010) was the framework for putting HSRA into action.

## Must-know facts
- Goals: better health outcomes, more responsive health systems, equitable health care financing.
- Four elements of the strategy (match each to its purpose):
  - Health financing: more, better and sustained investment in health (PhilHealth is the example).
  - Health regulation: quality and affordability of health goods and services.
  - Health service delivery: accessibility and availability of basic and essential care.
  - Good governance: better health system performance at national and local levels.
- DOH vision in the handout: Filipinos among the healthiest in Southeast Asia by 2022 and Asia by 2040. Mission: lead a productive, resilient, equitable, people-centered health system.
- DOH roles: leader in health (policy, plans, advocacy), enabler and capacity builder (oversight, quality standards), administrator of specific services (selected national hospitals, emergency response).

## How the exam asks about it
Given a program (for example, PhilHealth expansion), name which of the four elements it belongs to. Financing is the PhilHealth answer.

## Related topics
[[Department of Health (DOH) Concepts and Functions]], [[Local Health System and Inter-Local Health Zones]].

## Check against your textbook
Vision years and later frameworks (for example, universal health care) may have replaced these dates.
outlineRefs: Framework for the Implementation of HSRA

title: Local Health System and Inter-Local Health Zones
body:
## What it is
Under RA 7160 (Local Government Code), health structures, staff and budgets from the provincial level down to barangays were devolved to local government units (LGUs). The inter-local health zone (ILHZ) is the DOH-promoted system similar to a district health system.

## Must-know facts
- Objectives: set up a local health system, upgrade management and service capability of local facilities, promote inter-LGU links and cost sharing, involve the private sector, NGOs and community.
- Four parts of a health zone:
  - People: an ideal district serves about 100,000 to 500,000 for efficiency.
  - Boundaries: clear lines decide who is accountable.
  - Health facilities: district or provincial hospital and other services working as one integrated system.
  - Health workers: the right mix of providers for comprehensive services.

## Why it matters
Devolution made LGUs responsible for primary care, which is why the PHN works under the local government but follows DOH program protocols.

## Related topics
[[Health Sector Reform Agenda and FOURmula One]], [[Levels of Health Care and the Referral System]], [[Primary Health Care Basics]].

## Check against your textbook
Population size range is as given by the handout.

title: Levels of Health Care and the Referral System
body:
## What it is
Care is organized into three levels, and clients are referred upward when needs exceed what a facility can provide. Referral should be two-way: clients also return to the lower level for follow-up.

## Must-know facts
- Primary level: first contact, devolved to cities and municipalities. Staff: center physicians, public health nurses, rural health midwives, barangay health workers, traditional healers. Examples: barangay health station, rural health unit, health center, community hospital, puericulture center.
- Secondary level: physicians with basic training; referral center for primary facilities; can do minor surgery and simple laboratory tests. Examples: district or emergency hospital, provincial or city hospital.
- Tertiary level: specialists; handles complicated cases and intensive care; referral center for secondary facilities. Examples: regional and national medical centers, teaching hospitals.
- Primary health care worker levels: village or barangay health worker (trained community health worker, health auxiliary volunteer, traditional birth attendant or healer) and intermediate level (public health nurse, midwife, sanitary inspector, rural health physician).

## How the exam asks about it
Name the level of a given facility, or decide where to send a client: simple cases stay at primary; accompany the client during an emergency referral.

## Related topics
[[Primary Health Care Basics]], [[Primary Health Care Pillars and Characteristics]], [[Clinic Visit Standard Procedures]].

## Check against your textbook
Whether a community hospital counts as primary or secondary varies by source; the handout lists it under primary.
outlineRefs: Levels of Health Care and Health Referral System
Levels of Primary Health Care Worker

title: Management Functions of the Community Health Nurse
body:
## What it is
The CHN manages programs and people using six functions. Know them in order and what each means.

## Must-know facts
- Planning: build a vision, decide what must be done and what to achieve.
- Organizing: decide how to carry out the plan; analysis of systems and functions, assigning job responsibilities, implementation.
- Directing: tell workers what was decided in planning and organizing.
- Coordinating: link team members so objectives are met.
- Controlling: set standards, measure performance, correct deviations.
- Evaluating: judge effectiveness of actions by comparing results with a standard, to guide future decisions.

## How the exam asks about it
Scenarios: writing job descriptions is organizing; checking staff output against standards is controlling; holding a meeting to relay the plan is directing.

## Related topics
[[Family Nursing Process: Planning and Prioritization]], [[Public Health Nurse Roles and Qualifications]].
outlineRefs: Management Functions of the Community Health Nurse

title: Clinic Visit Standard Procedures
body:
## What it is
The standard flow a client follows in a health center, with the nurse managing program-based cases by protocol.

## Steps in order
1. Registration or admission: greet and build rapport, prepare a family record (new client) or retrieve it (old client), record chief complaint and history, do physical exam.
2. Waiting time: give priority numbers; first come first served, except emergencies.
3. Triaging: manage program-based cases per protocol, refer non-program cases to the physician, give first aid to emergencies.
4. Clinical evaluation: validate history and exam, reach an evidence-based diagnosis and treatment based on DOH programs, explain illness, treatment and prevention.
5. Laboratory and diagnostics: identify a designated referral laboratory when needed.
6. Referral: two-way referral; accompany the client in an emergency.
7. Prescription or dispensing: teach correct drug intake.
8. Health education: one-on-one counseling, reinforce messages, set the next appointment.

## Priority reasoning
Emergencies skip the queue (safety and ABC first). Everything else follows order of arrival.

## Related topics
[[Levels of Health Care and the Referral System]], [[Home Visit and Bag Technique]], [[Blood Pressure Measurement Technique]].

title: Blood Pressure Measurement Technique
body:
## What it is
Community-level BP measurement steps. Technique errors are a favorite exam target.

## Preparation
- Client relaxed and rested 5 minutes; no smoking or caffeine in the previous 30 minutes.
- Explain the procedure; seated or supine position.

## Applying equipment
- Bare the arm; cuff 2-3 cm above the brachial artery, snug without creases.
- Manometer at eye level; arm at heart level (supported on a table or chair arm; at the side if lying).
- Palpate the brachial pulse just below or slightly medial to the antecubital area.

## Palpatory then auscultatory
- Palpate: inflate until the pulse disappears; note that value as palpated systolic; deflate fully and wait 1-2 minutes.
- Auscultate: stethoscope over the brachial pulse; inflate to 30 mmHg above the palpated systolic; deflate slowly at 2-3 mmHg per beat.
- First clear tapping sound (Korotkoff phase I) is systolic; disappearance of sound (phase V) is diastolic.

## Recording
- At each visit, take the mean of 2 readings at least 2 minutes apart.
- First visit: measure both arms; later use the arm with the higher reading.

## Check against your textbook
The handout says "use the bell side" but then says the diaphragm for obese clients; most textbooks use the diaphragm for Korotkoff sounds and the bell for low sounds. Confirm which your school teaches.

## Related topics
[[Clinic Visit Standard Procedures]], [[Treatment of CD, NCD and Emergency Services]].

title: Home Visit and Bag Technique
body:
## What it is
A home visit is a professional family-nurse contact for assessing home and family situations and giving care. The bag technique is the method that keeps the visit efficient and prevents spread of infection.

## Home visit principles and purposes
- Must have a purpose; plan using available information, involve the family, prioritize essential needs.
- Purposes: give care, assess living conditions, teach prevention and control, link agencies and the public, use the referral system.
- Frequency depends on (most important first): family needs, then family acceptance, then agency policy, other agencies involved, past services, ability to recognize own needs.

## Steps
1. Greet and introduce self. 2. State purpose. 3. Observe and determine needs. 4. Place the bag in a convenient place and do the bag technique. 5. Give care and teaching. 6. Record. 7. Set a return visit.

## Bag technique
- Public health bag: essential equipment carried on every visit.
- Principles: minimize or prevent spread of infection; save time and effort; show total care effectiveness; may vary by agency or home as long as infection transfer is avoided.
- Bag contents: all needed supplies and emergency items, cleaned often and replaced, protected from contact with other articles, arranged for the user's convenience.

## Related topics
[[Family Nursing Process: Implementation and Evaluation]], [[Clinic Visit Standard Procedures]].

title: Maternal Health Program: Prenatal Visits, Supplements and Postpartum Care
body:
## What it is
The antenatal-to-postpartum service package under the family health program.

## Prenatal visit schedule
- 1st visit: as early in pregnancy as possible; 2nd: second trimester; 3rd: third trimester.
- After the 8th month: every 2 weeks until delivery.

## Micronutrient supplements (values as given in the handout)
- Vitamin A: 10,000 IU twice a week starting in the 4th month.
- Iron with folic acid: 60 mg/400 mcg tablet daily from the 5th month until 2 months postpartum.

## Other package items
- Treatment of diseases and conditions, clean and safe delivery.
- Teaching: birth registration, breastfeeding, newborn screening between 48 hours and 2 weeks of age.
- Postpartum visits: first in week one (preferably days 3-5), second at 6 weeks.
- Breastfeeding support and family planning counseling; spacing births 3-5 years.

## Related topics
[[Tetanus Toxoid Immunization]], [[Maternal and Child Health]], [[Newborn Screening]], [[Infant and Young Child Feeding]].

## Check against your textbook
Vitamin A dosing in pregnancy is highly source-dependent (and high doses can be harmful). Verify dose and timing with current DOH guidance before relying on this.

title: Family Planning Methods: Permanent, Hormonal and Barrier
body:
## Goal and role
Goal: universal access to FP information and services; helps couples reach desired family size under responsible parenthood and lowers infant, neonatal, under-five and maternal deaths. PHN roles: counseling, providing service packages, ensuring supplies. Common misconceptions: causes abortion, makes couples sterile, kills sexual desire.

## Methods
- Female sterilization (bilateral tubal ligation): permanent; fallopian tubes cut or blocked. Pros: no effect on sex or breastfeeding. Cons: surgical risks (infection, bleeding), ectopic pregnancy risk, hard to reverse, no STI protection.
- Male sterilization (vasectomy): vas deferens tied and cut or blocked via small scrotal opening. Effective after 3 months; mild pain and swelling 2-3 days; possible hematoma; reversal difficult and costly. Sexual ability and ejaculation are kept.
- Pill: estrogen and progesterone. Reduces painful menses and endometriosis symptoms; must be taken consistently; may cause nausea, dizziness, breast tenderness and can suppress lactation.
- Injectable: progestin; suppresses ovulation, thickens cervical mucus, alters uterine lining; reversible, no daily intake, no estrogen effects.
- Male condom: latex sheath; no hormones and protects against STIs; latex allergy or reduced sensation possible.
- LAM (lactational amenorrhea method): temporary postpartum method; works for a maximum of 6 months; effectiveness drops with separation or non-full breastfeeding.

## How the exam asks about it
Which method protects against STI (condom); which suppresses lactation (pill); LAM duration (6 months).

## Related topics
[[Fertility Awareness Family Planning Methods]], [[Reproductive Health and Family Planning]], [[Maternal and Child Health]].

## Check against your textbook
Combined pills are generally avoided in breastfeeding; confirm eligibility rules.

title: Fertility Awareness Family Planning Methods
body:
## What it is
Natural methods identify fertile days so the couple abstains (or uses a barrier) on those days. They need cooperation of both partners.

## Methods
- Mucus/billings method: abstain on fertile days based on cervical mucus. Unsuitable with unusual vaginal discharge.
- Basal body temperature: take temperature daily; a rise after ovulation marks the end of fertility. Handout figures: slight drop before ovulation and about 1 degree F rise at ovulation.
- Sympto-thermal: combines mucus, temperature and other ovulation signs.
- Two-day method: check for cervical secretions daily; any secretions today or yesterday mean fertile. Works for any cycle length, no cost, immediately reversible, involves the male partner; unreliable with abnormal secretions.
- Standard days method: color-coded cycle beads mark fertile and infertile days; no side effects; can avoid or achieve pregnancy.

## Cautions
- Not for women whose pregnancy would be dangerous (reliability matters).

## Check against your textbook
The handout says the standard days method "cannot be used by women who usually have cycles between 26 and 32 days"; this is reversed. It is meant for women whose cycles are usually 26-32 days long and is unsuitable outside that range.

## Related topics
[[Family Planning Methods: Permanent, Hormonal and Barrier]], [[Reproductive Health and Family Planning]].

title: Infant and Young Child Feeding
body:
## What it is
A child health program to improve nutrition of infants and young children and lower child mortality. It is one of the child health programs for ages 0-9, alongside newborn screening, immunization, childhood illness management, micronutrients, dental health, early child development and child injuries.

## Key messages
- Start breastfeeding within 1 hour of birth.
- Exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months: breast milk only, not even water.
- At 6 months add complementary foods that are timely, adequate, safe and properly fed.
- Continue breastfeeding to 2 years and beyond.
- Do not breastfeed when the mother has AIDS (handout position).

## Priority reasoning
Early skin-to-skin and early feeding support survival; teach before discharge.

## Related topics
[[Laws Protecting Infant Feeding and Food Fortification]], [[EINC and Active Management of Third Stage of Labor]], [[Nutrition]].

## Check against your textbook
HIV and breastfeeding advice varies with ART availability; verify current DOH policy.

title: Laws Protecting Infant Feeding and Food Fortification
body:
## Must-know laws
- Milk Code (EO 51): regulates breast milk substitutes including infant formula, other milk products and bottle-fed complementary foods.
- Rooming-In and Breastfeeding Act of 1992 (RA 7600): promotes rooming-in; mother and baby together for 24 hours (a step of baby-friendly hospitals).
- Food Fortification Law (RA 8976): mandatory fortification of rice, flour, edible oil and sugar; voluntary for processed foods.
- Expanded Breastfeeding Promotion Act of 2009 (RA 10028 in the handout): supports exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months.

## How the exam asks about it
Match law to topic: rooming-in (7600), fortification (8976), formula marketing (EO 51).

## Related topics
[[Infant and Young Child Feeding]], [[Nutrition]].

## Check against your textbook
The handout gives the year of RA 10028 as 2010; it is commonly dated 2009. Verify.
outlineRefs: Laws that Protect Infant and Young Child Feeding

title: Oral Health Program
body:
## What it is
A program to lower dental caries and periodontal disease. Handout targets: caries 92% (1998) to 85%, and periodontal disease 78% to 60% by 2010; 80% of children under 6 orally fit; better oral health for pregnant women and older persons.

## Classification of services
- Promotive: health education.
- Preventive: oral examination, oral hygiene, pit and fissure sealant, fluoride use.
- Curative: permanent and temporary fillings, atraumatic restorative treatment, gum treatment, extraction, post-extraction care, drainage of localized oral abscesses.

## How the exam asks about it
Sort an activity into promotive, preventive or curative. Sealants and fluoride are preventive.

## Related topics
[[Levels of Prevention]], [[Maternal and Child Health]].

title: Herbal Medicine: General Guidelines
body:
## What it is
Rules for safe use of medicinal plants in community health teaching.

## Must-know rules
- Use the right plant for the purpose and the suggested plant part, in the recommended dose.
- Use one kind of plant at a time.
- Stop if there is any untoward reaction.
- If no improvement after two or three doses, consult a physician.
- Boil in enamel or clay pots, not aluminum; clean the pot before and after.
- Avoid insecticide-treated plants.
- Wash and chop plants before boiling.

## Priority reasoning
Safety first: stop at adverse reaction and refer when no improvement; herbs do not replace medical care in serious illness.

## Related topics
[[Common Philippine Herbal Plants and Their Uses]], [[Essential Drugs]].
outlineRefs: General guidelines for the use of medicinal plants

title: Common Philippine Herbal Plants and Their Uses
body:
## What it is
Ten plants endorsed for community use. Memorize plant to use.

## Plant, use and preparation notes
- Lagundi (Vitex negundo): cough, asthma, fever. Boil chopped leaves in two cups of water 15 minutes on low fire; divide into three parts through the day (for fever, every four hours). Handout amounts: adult 6 tbsp fresh or 4 tbsp dried; ages 7-12 half of that; ages 2-6 about a quarter.
- Yerba buena: body pain. Boil, leave uncovered, cool and strain; drink in three parts; fresh crushed leaves may be applied to painful areas.
- Sambong (Blumea balsamifera): swelling, diuretic, helps urinary stones. Boil leaves uncovered.
- Tsaang gubat: stomachache. Divide into two parts, one part every four hours.
- Niyug-niyugan: ascariasis. Eat dried mature seeds two hours after supper; adult 8-10 seeds, fewer for children.
- Bayabas (guava): wound cleansing, mouth infection, swollen gums. Wash wounds twice a day; lukewarm solution as mouthwash.
- Akapulko (Cassia alata): infected skin, irritation, scabies. Apply squeezed leaf juice twice a day.
- Ulasimang bato: lowers uric acid; for arthritis and gout. Eat leaves as salad or take decoction.
- Bawang (garlic): lowers cholesterol. Two cloves with meals three times a day.
- Ampalaya: mild diabetes. Boil leaves 15 minutes; drink half a glass three times a day before meals.

## Check against your textbook
Doses are from the handout and are unverified; the DOH list also names plants such as these with different forms (for example, tablets). Check the official list.

## Related topics
[[Herbal Medicine: General Guidelines]].

title: Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Program
body:
## What it is
The program for preparing the public and strengthening the health sector to respond to emergencies and disasters. It stresses that emergencies need immediate response and are everyone's responsibility.

## Must-know facts
- Legal basis: PD 1566 (1978), strengthening disaster control and community disaster preparedness; RA 7160, which transferred responsibilities to LGUs.
- Disaster: serious disruption of society's functioning that exceeds its ability to cope with its own resources. Types by cause: natural or man-made. Hazard: any phenomenon that could disrupt or damage people and their environment.
- Main objective: decrease mortality and morbidity and prevent disability.
- Principles: first protect people at risk, second protect critical resources and systems; disaster management is part of national development, relies on understanding hazard risk, requires capabilities built before impact, and interdisciplinary collaboration.
- Major risks: natural (flood, earthquake, cyclone), technological, epidemics, societal (poverty, exclusion, group violence).

## Related topics
[[Disaster Nursing Basic Concepts]], [[Disaster Management Continuum]], [[NDRRMC and the Philippine Disaster Framework]].

## Check against your textbook
PD 1566 is old; current law is RA 10121 (see the NDRRMC note).
outlineRefs: Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Program

title: National Voluntary Blood Services Program
body:
## What it is
Program under the Blood Services Act (RA 7719, 1994) promoting voluntary, non-profit blood donation and a safe, adequate supply.

## Must-know facts
- Aims: encourage voluntary donation as a humanitarian act; provide safe, affordable, equitably distributed blood; involve all sectors.
- Donor requirements: age 16-65 (parental consent at 16-17), good health, weight over 45 kg for 250 mL or 50 kg for 450 mL, BP 90-160 systolic and 60-100 diastolic, hemoglobin at least 12.5 g/dL.
- Contraindications: diabetes, cancer, hyperthyroidism, cardiovascular, severe psychiatric, epilepsy, severe bronchitis, AIDS or syphilis and other STIs, malaria, kidney or liver disease, prolonged bleeding, prohibited drug use.
- Storage: whole blood and red cells up to 5 weeks; plasma frozen up to 12 months.

## Donor teaching after donation
- Keep the dressing on 3 to 12 hours; bruising is normal; avoid heavy lifting with that arm.
- No smoking for 2 hours, no alcohol for 12 hours; eat regular meals and drink more fluids.

## Related topics
[[Treatment of CD, NCD and Emergency Services]], [[Blood Pressure Measurement Technique]].

## Check against your textbook
Eligibility values vary by blood center.

title: Botika ng Barangay
body:
## What it is
A community drug store that supplies affordable, safe, essential medicines in remote and underserved areas, a partnership between the DOH and LGUs involving barangay health workers.

## Goal and objectives
- Ensure essential drugs are available and affordable, with priority for marginalized and hard-to-reach areas.
- Rationalize drug distribution; link DOH with LGUs; involve barangay health workers.

## Criteria for establishing one
- Run by a recognized community organization or cooperative with legal personality.
- Located in a far-flung, depressed or hard-to-reach barangay.
- Community-sourced funds of at least one third of initial capital, and the same from LGU or government sources.
- Barangay socio-economic and health profile, with list of indigents if available.
- Commitment of a licensed pharmacist to supervise.
- At least 2 accredited barangay health workers or volunteers trained as aides; designated space.

## Related topics
[[Essential Drugs]], [[Magna Carta of Public Health Workers]].

title: COPAR Ten Critical Activities and Participatory Action Research
body:
## What it is
Beyond the phases, COPAR uses ten recurring activities and a research approach where the community does the investigating.

## Ten critical activities
- Integration: living with and sharing the people's experience to build trust.
- Social investigation: systematic study of community structures and forces; gather geographic, economic, political and socio-cultural data, identify classes and sectors, decide approach.
- Planning: choose specific activities.
- Ground work (agitation): one-to-one motivation to act.
- Community meeting: ratifies decisions and gives collective power.
- Role play: rehearse the meeting with the target group.
- Social mobilization: people's action to solve their problems.
- Evaluation: what was done, left out, remains.
- Reflection: analyze strengths and weaknesses of finished action.
- Organization: widens participation and collective action.

## Participatory action research
- Beneficiaries are the main actors; blends education, research and action; purpose is empowerment.
- Versus traditional research: problems are defined by community members, not outside experts; the community runs the investigation with external researchers working alongside, and formulates its own recommendations.

## Related topics
[[Community Organizing (COPAR) Phases]], [[Community Organizing (COPAR) Basic Principles]].
